spoken.title: Trees in growing cities
spoken.text: When people discuss urban trees, they often begin with appearance. A street with trees looks more attractive than one without them. However, the value of trees extends well beyond decoration. Their shade keeps pavements and buildings cooler, while water released through their leaves helps cool the surrounding air. This matters especially in neighbourhoods with large areas of concrete and little open space. Trees can also make walking more comfortable, encouraging people to spend time outside and meet their neighbours. Yet planting a tree is only the beginning. A young tree needs suitable soil, enough space for its roots, and regular care while it becomes established. Choosing an unsuitable species can create problems for footpaths or water supplies. City planners therefore need to consider local conditions, future maintenance, and where shade is needed most. Involving residents can help because people who understand the benefits are more likely to support long-term care. The central point is that urban trees should be planned as useful infrastructure. A successful programme measures the health and survival of trees, rather than simply counting how many were planted.
keyPoints: Urban trees provide cooling and community benefits beyond appearance.
Suitable species, space and ongoing maintenance are necessary.
Planning should prioritise local needs, resident involvement and tree survival.
spoken.sample: The lecture explains that urban trees provide practical benefits, including cooling streets and encouraging outdoor social activity. However, successful planting requires suitable species, adequate root space and continuing maintenance. Planners should respond to local conditions and involve residents in tree care, evaluating programmes through tree health and survival rather than the number planted.

spoken.title: Learning by remembering
spoken.text: Many students prepare for examinations by reading the same notes repeatedly. This can make the material feel familiar, but familiarity is not the same as being able to explain it without help. One alternative is retrieval practice. After studying a topic, learners close their books and try to recall the main ideas, answer a question, or explain the concept to someone else. The purpose is not simply to discover a score. The attempt to remember helps learners recognise what they understand and what still needs attention. Feedback is essential because an incorrect answer should be checked and corrected before it becomes a habit. Timing also matters. Short periods of practice spread across several days give students opportunities to return to ideas after some forgetting has occurred. This can be more useful than concentrating all revision into one long session. Teachers can support the process with low-pressure questions at the beginning of a lesson and opportunities to discuss the answers afterwards. The important message is that effective revision involves actively using knowledge, checking mistakes, and revisiting material over time, rather than judging learning only by how familiar a page appears.
keyPoints: Familiarity from rereading is different from independently recalling knowledge.
Retrieval practice with corrective feedback reveals gaps in understanding.
Spaced, low-pressure practice supports effective revision.
spoken.sample: The speaker distinguishes familiarity from genuine recall and recommends retrieval practice instead of relying solely on rereading. Learners should remember or explain ideas without notes, then use feedback to correct mistakes and identify gaps. Spreading practice across several days and using low-pressure classroom questions helps students revisit and actively apply their knowledge over time.

spoken.title: Preventing household food waste
spoken.text: Household food waste is often described as a disposal problem, but much of the solution begins before food reaches the kitchen. Shopping without checking what is already available can lead to duplicate purchases. Special offers may also encourage people to buy more than they can reasonably use. A simple meal plan and a list based on existing supplies can reduce this problem. Once food is at home, storage and visibility become important. Items that are hidden at the back of a refrigerator are easily forgotten, so placing food that needs using soon in a visible area can help. Leftovers can be planned into another meal, provided they have been stored safely. However, advice must recognise that households differ. A rigid weekly plan may be difficult for someone working unpredictable hours or caring for family members. Flexible suggestions, such as keeping a small number of adaptable ingredients, may be more practical. Composting can deal with unavoidable scraps, but it does not recover all the resources used to produce food. Prevention should therefore come first, supported by shopping habits and storage routines that fit everyday life.
keyPoints: Food waste prevention starts with shopping and checking existing supplies.
Visible storage and planned use of leftovers reduce avoidable waste.
Flexible routines should fit different households; prevention comes before composting.
spoken.sample: The lecture argues that preventing household food waste begins with checking supplies and planning realistic purchases. Visible storage and safe use of leftovers can further reduce waste. Advice should accommodate different household routines through flexible meal planning and adaptable ingredients. Although composting handles unavoidable scraps, preventing waste better preserves the resources used in food production.

spoken.title: Making hybrid work effective
spoken.text: Hybrid work combines time in a shared workplace with time working elsewhere. It can give employees greater flexibility, but changing location alone does not guarantee better working conditions. Teams need to decide which activities benefit from being together and which can be completed independently. For example, an early discussion of an unfamiliar problem may benefit from direct conversation, while a task requiring sustained concentration may be easier in a quiet setting. Communication rules are equally important. If decisions are made informally by people in the office, remote colleagues may miss essential information. Recording decisions in a shared place and making meeting participation accessible can reduce this imbalance. Managers also need to judge work through agreed outcomes rather than simply noticing who is physically present. At the same time, flexibility should not mean that employees must be available at every hour. Clear expectations about response times and working hours help protect boundaries. The main lesson is that hybrid arrangements work best when they are designed around tasks, fair access to information, and clear expectations. There is no single schedule that will suit every team.
keyPoints: Hybrid arrangements should match tasks rather than apply one universal schedule.
Shared decisions and accessible meetings support fairness for remote staff.
Outcome-based management and clear working boundaries are necessary.
spoken.sample: The speaker explains that effective hybrid work requires more than flexible locations. Teams should match workplace attendance to tasks, share decisions clearly and make meetings accessible to remote colleagues. Managers should assess agreed outcomes and establish expectations about availability. Successful arrangements therefore depend on fair communication, suitable working conditions and boundaries tailored to each team.

spoken.title: Museums and community stories
spoken.text: A museum collection can tell us about the past, but the meaning of an object is not always obvious from its appearance. A simple tool may reveal little until someone explains who used it, how it was made, and why it mattered in everyday life. This is one reason museums increasingly invite communities to contribute stories as well as objects. Personal accounts can connect a collection to experiences that formal records overlook. However, collecting a story creates responsibilities. Contributors should understand how their words will be used, and museums should distinguish personal memories from independently verified facts. Different people may remember the same event in different ways. Presenting these differences carefully can encourage visitors to think about how historical knowledge is constructed. Digital recordings can make stories available to wider audiences, but they also require attention to accessibility and long-term preservation. A recording is of limited value if future visitors cannot open it or understand it. Community participation therefore involves an ongoing relationship. Museums need to combine professional care with respect for contributors, allowing collections to represent a broader range of experiences without abandoning careful interpretation.
keyPoints: Community stories give objects context and include experiences missing from formal records.
Consent and careful distinction between memory and verified fact are essential.
Accessible preservation and continuing community relationships support responsible interpretation.
spoken.sample: The lecture describes how community stories give museum objects context and represent experiences overlooked by formal records. Museums must obtain informed participation, distinguish memories from verified facts and present differing accounts carefully. Digital access also requires preservation and accessibility. Combining professional interpretation with respect for contributors makes community involvement an ongoing relationship rather than a single collection activity.

questions.title: Public libraries
questions.text:
Public libraries are often associated with shelves of books, yet their role is changing as information becomes increasingly available online. Some observers assume that digital access makes physical libraries unnecessary. This view overlooks the difference between the availability of information and the ability to use it effectively. People may lack reliable internet connections, appropriate devices, or the skills needed to assess competing claims. Libraries can help address these gaps by providing equipment and guidance in an accessible public setting.

Their buildings also offer resources that a website cannot fully replace. Quiet study areas support learners whose homes are crowded, while group spaces allow local organisations to meet. Staff may help visitors locate services or navigate unfamiliar information systems. These activities extend the traditional purpose of enabling people to learn and participate in society.

However, expanding services creates practical choices. Funding, staff time and building space are limited. A library that attempts every possible activity may weaken its essential services. Decisions should therefore be based on local needs and regular consultation with users, including people who rarely visit. The future of libraries is best understood as adaptation: combining books, digital support and shared space in ways that make knowledge genuinely accessible.
keyPoints: Libraries remain relevant by addressing unequal access to information and digital skills.
Physical spaces support learning and community participation.
Services should adapt to local needs within resource limits.
questions.sample: Public libraries remain important by combining books, digital guidance and shared spaces to improve access to knowledge and community participation, although limited resources require them to adapt services carefully to local needs.

questions.title: Repairable products
questions.text:
Replacing a broken household appliance can appear easier than repairing it. If spare parts are unavailable, technical information is difficult to obtain, or a product is sealed in a way that prevents safe access, even a minor fault may lead to disposal. This means that the lifespan of a product depends partly on decisions made long before the customer buys it. Design can either support repair or make it impractical.

A repairable product uses components that can be reached and replaced, supported by instructions and a reliable supply of parts. Such arrangements can allow equipment to remain useful for longer and reduce demand for new materials. They may also support local repair businesses. Nevertheless, repairability alone does not guarantee that repairs will occur. Customers compare costs, time and confidence in the result. If the total repair price approaches the cost of a replacement, the environmental argument may not determine the decision.

Encouraging repair therefore requires cooperation across the product's life. Manufacturers influence design and spare parts, repair services provide expertise, and consumers need clear information about practical options. The aim is not to insist that every damaged item must be repaired, but to make repair a realistic choice when it is safe and worthwhile.
keyPoints: Design and spare-part availability shape product repairability and lifespan.
Repair can conserve materials and support local services, but cost and confidence affect choices.
Cooperation should make safe, worthwhile repairs practical.
questions.sample: Making household products repairable through accessible design, spare parts and reliable information can extend their lives and conserve materials, but manufacturers, repair services and consumers must also address cost and confidence to make safe repairs a practical choice.

questions.title: Age Restrictions
questions.text: Age restrictions are placed on many activities. It is believed that people should not do things until they reach the right ages, such as getting married, driving, voting, buying certain products, and doing particular things. Give an example, state which minimum age you think it should be and share your own experience.
keyPoints: Choose a specific activity affected by age restrictions.
State and justify a suitable minimum age for that activity.
Share relevant personal experience and connect it to the chosen age restriction.
One well-developed example is sufficient; the response does not need to discuss every activity listed in the question.
questions.sample:
Age restrictions can protect people when an activity requires judgement and responsibility. One important example is independent driving, because a driver's decisions affect passengers, pedestrians and other road users. I believe eighteen is a suitable minimum age for driving without supervision, provided the learner has also completed practical training and demonstrated safe driving skills.

The main reason for choosing this age is that independent driving involves much more than controlling a vehicle. A driver must assess changing conditions, resist distractions and consider the consequences of taking risks. By eighteen, many young people have gained greater experience managing responsibilities at school, at work or at home. However, age alone cannot guarantee sensible behaviour. A clear minimum age should therefore be combined with supervised practice, a practical assessment and education about dangerous situations. This would make the restriction meaningful rather than simply treating a birthday as proof of readiness.

My own experience of learning to drive showed me why preparation matters. During my early lessons, I could follow basic instructions but found busy intersections difficult. Regular practice with an experienced instructor helped me anticipate other drivers' actions and remain calm when conditions changed. If I had driven alone before developing these habits, I would have felt less confident and might have made avoidable mistakes. This experience supports allowing young people to learn under supervision before they become eligible to drive independently.

In conclusion, I would set eighteen as the minimum age for independent driving. Combining this age restriction with training and demonstrated competence would balance young people's independence with their responsibility to protect others.

questions.title: Designing quiet learning spaces
questions.text: When a university plans a learning space, the discussion often begins with furniture and technology. Yet sound can have just as much influence on how people use the room. A conversation that helps one group solve a problem may interrupt another student who is trying to read. The answer is not necessarily to make every room silent. Different activities require different conditions. A useful building can offer separate areas for discussion, individual concentration and short informal meetings. Clear signs help students choose a suitable place, but the physical design must support those expectations. Soft surfaces can reduce echoes, while doors and partitions can limit sound travelling between areas. Location matters too. A quiet study zone beside a busy entrance may be difficult to protect, regardless of how many notices are displayed. Planners should also listen to students who have particular difficulties processing speech in noisy environments. Their experience can reveal problems that a simple sound measurement misses. Finally, spaces should be reviewed after they open. Observing actual use and inviting feedback allows the university to adjust layouts and rules as learning needs change.
keyPoints: Learning spaces need different sound conditions for different activities.
Physical design and location must support quiet and collaborative areas.
Student feedback and continuing evaluation help meet diverse learning needs.
questions.sample: The lecture explains that university learning spaces should provide different sound conditions for discussion and individual concentration. Effective planning combines clear expectations with suitable locations, partitions and materials that reduce unwanted noise. Universities should consult students with different listening needs and review how rooms are used, adjusting layouts and rules in response to continuing feedback.

questions.title: Citizen science
questions.text:
Scientific projects sometimes require observations from more places and over longer periods than a small research team can cover. Citizen science offers one way to meet this challenge by inviting members of the public to contribute observations. Volunteers might record flowering times, report wildlife sightings or classify images. Their participation can extend the reach of a project while creating opportunities to learn about scientific methods.

The usefulness of these contributions depends on how the work is organised. A large number of observations does not automatically produce reliable evidence. Participants need clear instructions, suitable training and a way to report uncertainty. Researchers must also check records and consider whether volunteers are concentrated in particular areas. Otherwise, an apparent pattern may reflect where people looked rather than what is happening in nature.

Successful projects treat communication as a continuing process. Explaining why an observation matters can improve engagement, and sharing findings helps contributors see the value of their effort. Volunteers should also receive appropriate recognition. Citizen science is therefore more than a source of inexpensive labour. When carefully designed, it combines wider data collection with public involvement, while maintaining the standards needed for useful research.
keyPoints: Public participation extends scientific observation and learning.
Training, verification and attention to sampling bias are necessary for reliable data.
Ongoing communication and recognition make citizen science a meaningful partnership.
questions.sample: Citizen science can expand data collection and public learning, provided projects use clear training, verification and checks for sampling bias, while continuing communication and recognition help maintain meaningful participation and reliable research.

questions.title: Reliable public transport
questions.text:
Discussions about public transport often concentrate on the speed of a journey. A faster train or a shorter bus route seems an obvious improvement. Yet passengers also care about whether the journey will take roughly the time they expect. An unusually fast trip on one day may offer little reassurance if the service is frequently delayed on others. Reliability influences the extra time people allow when travelling to work, education or appointments.

Transport authorities can improve reliability through measures that receive less attention than new vehicles. Bus priority at busy intersections, realistic timetables and well-planned connections can make existing services more dependable. Accurate information is also useful when disruptions occur, because passengers can make alternative arrangements. However, information cannot compensate indefinitely for a service that fails to arrive.

Different travellers experience unreliability differently. Someone who can change their working hours may manage a delay more easily than a person collecting a child at a fixed time. Evaluating improvements should therefore include passengers' experiences as well as average journey times. A useful transport system is one people can plan their lives around; its value comes from consistent service, accessible information and an understanding of everyday travel needs.
keyPoints: Predictability matters alongside speed because passengers plan around journeys.
Operational improvements and accurate disruption information can help reliability.
Evaluation should consider differing passenger needs, not only average travel times.
questions.sample: Reliable public transport enables people to plan daily activities, so authorities should complement speed improvements with dependable operations and accurate information, evaluating services against different passengers' needs as well as average journey times.

questions.title: Late Submission and Mark Deduction
questions.text: Some universities deduct marks from students' work if it is given in late. What is your opinion? Suggest some alternative actions.
keyPoints: Give and explain an opinion about deducting marks for late university submissions.
Suggest relevant alternative actions and explain how they would work.
Support the discussion with reasons or examples; personal experience is optional.
questions.sample:
Deadlines are an important part of university assessment because they help students organise their work and allow teachers to provide feedback fairly. Although deducting marks can encourage timely submission, I believe penalties should be proportionate and should take genuine difficulties into account. Universities should also use practical alternatives that help students meet deadlines.

A reasonable deduction may be justified when a student submits work late without an acceptable explanation. Students who complete an assignment on time have managed within the same stated conditions, so unlimited extra time could create an unfair advantage. A published penalty also makes expectations clear. However, automatically applying the same deduction to every case can be unreasonable. Illness, caring responsibilities or an unexpected technical problem may prevent a capable student from submitting on time. In such circumstances, a severe penalty could obscure what the student actually understands about the subject.

Several alternative actions could support both fairness and learning. First, universities could offer short extensions when students explain their circumstances and provide appropriate evidence. Second, a limited grace period for occasional minor delays could prevent a small mistake from causing a disproportionate academic loss. Third, teachers could divide major assignments into planning, draft and final submission stages. These checkpoints would identify difficulties early and encourage steady progress. Students who repeatedly miss deadlines could attend time management sessions or agree on an improvement plan with an adviser.

In conclusion, moderate mark deductions can be appropriate for unexplained late submissions, but they should not be the only response. Clear extension procedures, early checkpoints and targeted support would maintain academic expectations while addressing the reasons students fall behind.

questions.title: Explaining uncertainty in research
questions.text: When researchers communicate a result, people often want a single clear answer. However, scientific findings usually come with some uncertainty. This does not automatically mean that the research is poor. A study may involve only a sample of a larger population, and measurements can be affected by small variations in the equipment or the conditions. Responsible researchers explain these limitations so that others can judge how much confidence to place in the findings. The challenge is to communicate uncertainty without making useful evidence seem meaningless. Simply listing technical qualifications can overwhelm an audience. It is often better to explain what the study supports, what it cannot establish, and which further observations would help. Comparisons with other studies are also valuable. A result becomes more convincing when different methods produce similar conclusions, although agreement does not remove the need for critical examination. Communicators should avoid presenting an early finding as a final discovery, particularly when decisions could affect many people. At the same time, waiting for perfect certainty may delay worthwhile action. The aim is to make decisions that reflect the strength of the available evidence while remaining open to revision.
keyPoints: Uncertainty is normal because studies use samples and imperfect measurements.
Researchers should explain both findings and limitations in accessible language.
Decisions should reflect available evidence, comparison across studies and openness to revision.
questions.sample: The speaker explains that uncertainty is a normal feature of scientific research, arising from sampling and measurement limitations. Researchers should clearly communicate what findings support and what remains unknown, while considering evidence from other studies. Decisions should reflect the strength of available knowledge without treating early results as final or waiting indefinitely for perfect certainty.

predictionEssays.title: Television as a Relaxation Tool and Companion
predictionEssays.text: Television serves many useful functions. It helps people to relax. Besides, it can also be seen as a companion for the lonely. To what extent do you agree with this? Explain why with your own experience.
keyPoints: Give a clear view about television as a relaxation tool and companion.
Explain how suitable programmes can reduce stress or provide entertainment.
Discuss the limits of television as a substitute for genuine relationships.
Use relevant personal experience or an example to support the position.
predictionEssays.sample:
Television can help people relax and can provide a sense of companionship, but I only partly agree that these are always useful functions. Its value depends on the programme, the amount of time spent watching and whether it supplements rather than replaces real relationships.

After a demanding day, a comedy, documentary or familiar series can give viewers a simple mental break. This kind of entertainment may reduce stress and help people shift their attention away from work or study. Television can also make a quiet home feel less empty. For example, an older person living alone may enjoy hearing presenters discuss everyday issues and may feel connected to a wider community.

However, television is not a true substitute for friendship. A viewer cannot receive personal advice, share responsibilities or develop mutual understanding with a programme. Excessive viewing may also reduce exercise, sleep and face-to-face conversation. Someone who watches television whenever they feel lonely might temporarily feel better while becoming even more isolated in the long term.

In my own experience, watching a short programme with my family helps us relax together because it creates a topic for conversation. By contrast, watching alone late at night often leaves me tired rather than refreshed. Therefore, television is a useful relaxation tool and limited companion, but people should combine it with active hobbies and genuine social contact.

predictionEssays.title: Studying Old Plays and Theatre Works
predictionEssays.text: What are the problems and the benefits for high school students of studying plays and other works for theatre that were written centuries ago? Do you agree with it? Use your own experience to discuss it.
keyPoints: Address both the benefits and the problems of studying historical theatre.
Explain how old plays can develop language, cultural understanding or critical thinking.
Explain difficulties such as unfamiliar language or distant social values.
State whether high school students should study these works and support the view with experience.
predictionEssays.sample:
High school students can benefit from studying plays written centuries ago, although the material should be introduced with suitable guidance. I agree with including historical theatre because it develops more than literary knowledge, but it should not replace exposure to contemporary works.

Old plays give students an opportunity to examine how people in another period understood family, power, justice and social responsibility. Their language and dramatic structure can also improve reading skills, interpretation and confidence in discussing different viewpoints. When students perform a scene, they must understand the characters' motives and communicate meaning through voice and movement. This makes literature more active than simply memorising information.

The main difficulty is that historical works may contain unfamiliar vocabulary, cultural references and attitudes that modern students find confusing or unacceptable. Without explanation, a class may focus on translating difficult sentences instead of considering the ideas. Some learners may also believe that old stories have no connection with their lives. Teachers can address these problems by providing context, comparing the original work with a modern adaptation and inviting students to question outdated assumptions.

In my own experience, discussing an older play became interesting when my class performed selected scenes and compared the characters' choices with situations today. I realised that the setting was distant, but the conflict about responsibility was still understandable. Therefore, historical theatre deserves a place in high school education when it is taught alongside modern voices and connected to students' experiences.

predictionEssays.title: Combining Study and Employment
predictionEssays.text: Effective study requires time, comfort and peace. It is impossible to study with employment because one may distract the other. To what extent do you think the statements are realistic? Give your opinion with examples.
keyPoints: Give a clear opinion about whether employment and effective study can coexist.
Discuss how employment can create time pressure, tiredness or distraction.
Explain possible benefits such as discipline, income and practical skills.
Support the view with realistic examples and conditions for success.
predictionEssays.sample:
The claim that employment makes effective study impossible is too absolute. Working while studying can create serious pressure, but many students can manage both when their hours are limited and their schedules are organised carefully.

Employment may reduce the time and energy available for academic work. A student who finishes a late shift may struggle to concentrate during an early lecture or may postpone important assignments. Unpredictable rosters can be especially damaging because the learner cannot plan regular revision. Financial concerns may also distract students from their studies. These problems show why full-time employment is often unsuitable during demanding courses.

Nevertheless, part-time work can provide useful advantages. Earning an income may reduce dependence on family members and allow a student to pay for transport, books or accommodation. A job can also develop punctuality, communication and problem-solving skills. For instance, a student working several fixed hours in a shop may learn to plan study periods efficiently and become more disciplined about deadlines.

In my experience, combining study with a small weekend job was manageable because my shifts were predictable. I reserved weekday evenings for reading and began assignments before they became urgent. The arrangement became difficult only when I accepted extra shifts during examination periods. This taught me that the number and timing of hours matter more than employment itself. Therefore, study and employment can coexist, provided students have realistic workloads, protected study time and an employer willing to respect their academic commitments.

predictionEssays.title: Experiential Learning in Education
predictionEssays.text: Some people point that experiential learning (i.e. learning by doing it) can work well in formal education. However, others think a traditional form of teaching is the best. Do you think experiential learning can work well in high schools or colleges?
keyPoints: State whether experiential learning works effectively in formal education.
Explain how practical activities can deepen understanding and build transferable skills.
Acknowledge the value of direct instruction for foundations and difficult concepts.
Give a relevant school or college example.
predictionEssays.sample:
Experiential learning can work very well in high schools and colleges, but it should complement rather than completely replace traditional teaching. Students need explanations and background knowledge before they can benefit fully from practical activities.

Learning by doing makes abstract information easier to understand. A biology student who grows plants can observe how light, water and soil affect development instead of only reading about these factors. Similarly, a business student who runs a small project must communicate with others, manage resources and respond to unexpected problems. Such activities develop judgement, cooperation and the ability to apply knowledge in unfamiliar situations. They can also make lessons more memorable and motivate students who struggle with passive note-taking.

Traditional instruction remains important because teachers can introduce accurate concepts efficiently and correct misunderstandings before they become habits. A practical experiment without clear guidance may produce a confusing result, and some subjects require substantial theoretical preparation. Experiential tasks can also be expensive or difficult to organise if schools lack equipment and safe facilities.

In my own education, a group project on reducing classroom waste helped me understand environmental principles more clearly than a textbook chapter alone. We collected observations, proposed changes and evaluated what happened, while our teacher explained the relevant concepts. The theory gave direction to the activity, and the activity gave meaning to the theory. Therefore, formal education should combine clear instruction with carefully designed experiences that allow students to apply, test and reflect on what they learn.

predictionEssays.title: Digital Materials and Libraries
predictionEssays.text: With the increase of new digital media available online, the role of the library has become obsolete. Therefore universities should only procure digital materials rather than constantly update textbooks. Discuss both the advantages and disadvantages of this position and give your own point of view.
keyPoints: Discuss advantages and disadvantages of replacing physical materials with digital resources.
Explain benefits such as convenient access, searchability and lower distribution costs.
Explain limits including unequal access, screen fatigue, unreliable information and loss of shared space.
Give a clear view about whether universities should use digital-only procurement.
predictionEssays.sample:
Digital materials have transformed university study, but they have not made libraries or updated textbooks obsolete. In my view, universities should expand digital collections while maintaining carefully selected physical resources and welcoming library spaces.

Online books and journals are convenient because students can search them quickly and access them from home at any time. Digital copies also occupy little physical space and can be updated more easily when research changes. A university may serve learners on different campuses without transporting large numbers of books. Search tools, adjustable text and audio features can further support students with different learning needs.

However, digital-only procurement has important disadvantages. Not every student has a reliable internet connection, a suitable device or a quiet place to study. Long periods of screen use may cause fatigue, and some learners understand complex arguments better when they can annotate a printed page. Online information also varies in quality, so students still need librarians and teachers to evaluate sources. If libraries lose their physical collections and study areas, students may lose an accessible place for concentration and academic discussion.

During my own studies, electronic articles were useful for quick research, but I preferred printed chapters when preparing for an examination because I could concentrate and remember the structure more easily. This experience showed me that the two formats serve different purposes. Universities should therefore invest in both systems, using digital access for flexibility and libraries for reliable guidance, focused study and equal educational opportunity.

predictionEssays.title: Public Transport and Road Building
predictionEssays.text: As cities expand, governments should look forward to creating better networks of public transport available for everyone rather than building more roads for vehicle owning population. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
keyPoints: State the extent to which governments should prioritise public transport over additional roads.
Explain how accessible transport can reduce congestion, pollution and dependence on private cars.
Acknowledge situations where road investment remains necessary.
Support the position with practical urban examples.
predictionEssays.sample:
As cities grow, governments should give priority to reliable and affordable public transport rather than continually adding roads for private vehicles. Roads will still be necessary for deliveries, emergency services and areas that cannot be served efficiently by rail or buses, but transport policy should focus on moving people efficiently.

A strong public transport network allows many residents to travel without owning a car. Frequent buses, trains and safe connections can reduce the number of vehicles on congested streets and lower pollution caused by traffic. They also improve access to employment and education for people who cannot afford a private vehicle, including young people, older residents and low-income workers. If services are frequent and dependable, commuters may choose them voluntarily instead of seeing them as a second-rate option.

Building more roads can provide short-term relief, but it often encourages more people to drive. New lanes may become crowded again as residents change their travel habits and housing expands around car access. Road construction also consumes valuable land that could be used for homes, parks or community facilities. Nevertheless, some road maintenance and targeted improvements are essential, particularly in outer suburbs where public transport is not yet practical.

In my experience, I am more willing to leave a car at home when a bus arrives regularly and connects smoothly with another service. This shows that convenience is central to behaviour. Therefore, governments should invest mainly in integrated public transport while making selective road improvements where they serve essential local needs.

predictionEssays.title: Tourism in Less Developed Countries
predictionEssays.text: For a less developed country, the disadvantages of tourism are as great as the advantages. Please discuss this statement, and give and explain your opinion.
keyPoints: Discuss both the benefits and disadvantages of tourism for less developed countries.
Explain benefits such as employment, income, infrastructure and cultural exchange.
Explain risks such as environmental damage, inequality, cultural pressure and dependence.
Give a reasoned opinion about whether the disadvantages are equally great.
predictionEssays.sample:
Tourism can bring major benefits to a less developed country, but it can also create serious economic, social and environmental problems. I do not believe the disadvantages are automatically as great as the advantages; their balance depends on how tourism is planned and who controls its benefits.

Visitors create demand for accommodation, food, transport, guides and cultural activities. This can provide employment and income for local families, while taxes may help governments improve roads, airports and public services. Tourism can also encourage residents to protect historic places and natural landscapes because these attractions have continuing value. Contact with visitors may promote cultural exchange and help a country become better known internationally.

Uncontrolled tourism, however, can damage the very resources that attract visitors. Large resorts may consume water, produce waste and restrict local access to beaches or forests. Profits may leave the country if hotels and tour companies are owned by foreign corporations. Popular destinations can also experience higher prices, seasonal employment and pressure to present simplified versions of their culture. If a country depends too heavily on visitors, an economic crisis or natural disaster can quickly reduce national income.

In my opinion, responsible tourism offers greater benefits when communities participate in decisions and receive a fair share of revenue. Governments should limit development in sensitive areas, enforce environmental standards and support locally owned businesses. Tourism is therefore neither wholly beneficial nor equally harmful; with careful regulation, it can support development without sacrificing local wellbeing or cultural independence.

predictionEssays.title: Formal Written Examinations
predictionEssays.text: Many education systems assess students' learning using formal written examinations. Those kinds of exams are a valid method. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give examples with your own experience.
keyPoints: State the extent to which formal written examinations are a valid assessment method.
Explain benefits such as common conditions, individual accountability and coverage of knowledge.
Explain limitations including anxiety, narrow skills and one-day performance.
Use a relevant example or personal experience to support the view.
predictionEssays.sample:
Formal written examinations are a valid way to assess some aspects of learning, but they should not be the only method used by education systems. A balanced approach can measure academic knowledge while also recognising practical and collaborative abilities.

Examinations provide a common structure for comparing students. When learners answer questions independently under the same conditions, teachers can see whether they understand key concepts without relying entirely on group contributions. A well-designed paper can cover a broad part of a course and encourage students to revise regularly. Written answers may also reveal how clearly a learner can organise an argument and apply information to a new problem.

Nevertheless, examinations have significant weaknesses. Some capable students perform poorly because of severe anxiety, illness or unfamiliar testing conditions. A timed paper may reward memorisation more than creativity, communication or practical skill. It also represents performance on one particular day, so it may not reflect a student's usual effort or understanding. For subjects such as science, design and language, projects, presentations and observed tasks can provide evidence that a written paper cannot capture.

In my own experience, examinations helped me identify which theories I needed to review, but a research project showed my ability to find sources, solve problems and work consistently over several weeks. Neither assessment alone gave a complete picture. Therefore, formal written examinations are useful when they are fair and carefully designed, but schools and universities should combine them with coursework and practical assessment to evaluate learning more accurately.

predictionEssays.title: Compulsory Foreign Language Learning

Acknowledge practical concerns including timetable pressure, resources and different student abilities.

predictionEssays.sample: Learning a foreign language should be compulsory at school because it develops communication skills, cultural awareness and future opportunities. However, compulsory study should be flexible enough to support students who learn at different speeds or have particular educational needs. A second language gives young people a practical way to communicate with visitors, international classmates and future colleagues. It also introduces them to different traditions and ways of thinking, which can reduce prejudice and improve cooperation. In an increasingly connected economy, employers may value workers who can deal with customers or partners from other countries. Early language education is especially useful because children are generally able to develop pronunciation and confidence before fear of making mistakes becomes a major barrier. There are nevertheless challenges. Some schools do not have enough qualified teachers, and students may already face heavy academic demands. If every learner is judged by an identical target, those who need additional support could become discouraged. Language lessons should therefore emphasise steady progress and everyday communication instead of relying only on difficult examinations. When I studied another language, regular conversations and simple cultural projects were more motivating than memorising long vocabulary lists. The subject helped me communicate with international students and made travel less intimidating. Foreign-language learning should consequently be compulsory, with appropriate support and assessment that recognises gradual improvement rather than demanding identical results from everyone.

These events can destroy infrastructure and force people to leave their communities. Changes in rainfall also make farming less predictable, which may raise food prices and intensify competition for resources. Poorer countries are particularly vulnerable because they often have fewer funds to protect cities or recover from disasters, even though their historical emissions may be relatively small. The first solution is a rapid reduction in greenhouse-gas emissions. Governments should expand renewable energy, improve electricity networks, set realistic efficiency standards and provide reliable public transport. Companies must measure their emissions and redesign production rather than treating environmental action as a marketing exercise. International organisations can help by directing finance and technical knowledge to developing countries, while wealthier nations should support adaptation in vulnerable regions. Individuals also have a role through efficient energy use, lower-waste consumption and informed political choices, but personal action cannot replace structural reform. Coordinated government policy is the essential starting point because it changes the incentives facing millions of households and businesses.

predictionEssays.title: Medical Technology and Life Expectancy
predictionEssays.text: The medical technology can increase the average life expectancy. Do you think it is a curse or a blessing?
keyPoints: Clearly decide whether longer life through medical technology is mainly a blessing or a curse.

Acknowledge concerns including unequal access, ageing populations and longer periods of illness.

predictionEssays.sample: Medical technology that increases average life expectancy is mainly a blessing, provided that longer lives are supported by good health services and social planning. New treatments can prevent suffering and give people more years with their families, although the benefits are not automatically shared equally. Advances in screening, surgery, medicines and assistive devices allow doctors to identify illnesses earlier and manage conditions that were once fatal. A person with a serious disease may now recover, remain independent or continue working and contributing to the community. Longer lifespans also allow grandparents to support younger relatives and give individuals more time to pursue education, relationships and meaningful interests. There are genuine difficulties. If people live longer without adequate prevention or aged-care services, they may spend many years with chronic illness. An ageing population can place pressure on pensions, hospitals and younger workers. Expensive treatments may also be available mainly to wealthy patients or countries, widening health inequalities. These problems show the need for planning rather than proving that longer life is harmful in itself. Routine tests and improved treatments have helped people I know manage conditions that previously would have shortened their lives. Governments should therefore invest in prevention, affordable primary care, healthy ageing and ethical access to innovation. Medical technology is a blessing when it extends healthy, dignified life instead of simply prolonging dependence without support.

predictionEssays.title: Parental Legal Responsibility
predictionEssays.text: Should parents be held legally responsible for the actions of their children? Support your opinion from your study, observations or experiences.
keyPoints: State when parents should or should not be legally responsible for a child's actions.
Explain how supervision, guidance and reasonable prevention can influence responsibility.
Distinguish deliberate neglect from behaviour that parents could not reasonably control.
Use an observation, study or experience to support the position.
predictionEssays.sample: Parents should be held legally responsible for a child's actions only when their serious neglect or deliberate encouragement contributed to the harm. Making parents automatically liable for every mistake would be unfair because children gradually develop independence and cannot always be controlled. Adults have a duty to provide reasonable supervision, teach safe behaviour and respond when they know that a child is repeatedly causing danger. For instance, a parent who allows an unsupervised child to drive, stores a dangerous weapon carelessly or ignores clear warnings about repeated vandalism may have failed to prevent foreseeable harm. In such situations, legal responsibility can encourage families to take supervision and education seriously. However, children are not simply extensions of their parents. As they grow older, they make independent decisions at school, online and with friends. Even attentive parents cannot observe every conversation or predict every impulsive act. Automatic penalties could also punish families who are already dealing with poverty, disability or limited access to support, without addressing the child's actual needs. The young person should be accountable in an age-appropriate way, while parents should be assessed according to what they reasonably knew and could have done. In my observation, parents who set consistent boundaries and discuss consequences often help children correct harmful behaviour, but they cannot prevent every poor choice. The law should therefore focus on evidence of negligence, encouragement or failure to act after a known risk.

In contrast, small rooms, inadequate ventilation and constant artificial light may affect physical and mental wellbeing. Architects and developers should therefore evaluate buildings through the experience of their users, not just their visual style. Thoughtful design can make everyday environments healthier, more inclusive and more efficient.

predictionEssays.title: Modern Inventions and Their Impact

predictionEssays.sample: One important modern invention is the portable artificial-intelligence medical assistant, which can analyse symptoms, images and health records to help clinicians identify disease earlier. It can also reduce routine paperwork, allowing doctors and nurses to spend more time speaking with patients. These concerns require strong privacy rules, independent testing, human oversight and transparent information about limitations. The invention should therefore support, rather than replace, trained medical professionals. If hospitals validate its recommendations and governments ensure fair access, it can extend expert knowledge to underserved areas and improve early treatment. Its impact is ultimately beneficial because the dangers arise from careless implementation, not from the idea of using technology to assist diagnosis.

predictionEssays.title: Workers in Decision-Making
predictionEssays.text: In some companies, employers involve workers in decision-making process about products and services. What are the advantages and disadvantages of such a policy?
keyPoints: Discuss both advantages and disadvantages of involving employees in product and service decisions.

predictionEssays.sample: Involving workers in decisions about products and services can improve a company's performance, but it also creates risks if roles and authority are unclear. The policy is most effective when employees contribute relevant knowledge within a structured decision-making process. Front-line workers often understand customer complaints, technical difficulties and practical operating costs better than senior managers do. Their suggestions may reveal a problem before it becomes expensive or identify a feature that customers genuinely need. Participation can also increase motivation because employees see that their experience is respected. Employees may focus on the needs of their own team rather than the organisation's long-term strategy. Managers remain accountable for legal, financial and strategic outcomes, so involving staff should not make responsibility impossible to identify. A practical solution is to create representative working groups, provide the necessary evidence and set a clear deadline for recommendations. Management can then explain which suggestions were adopted and why other proposals were rejected. In my experience, group decisions are strongest when people who use a process daily are consulted, while one person remains responsible for coordinating the final choice. Employee participation should therefore be encouraged, especially for customer-facing improvements, but it needs clear boundaries, confidentiality and accountable leadership.
